rationale: The book's case is coherent and strong against reading the oil of the ten virgins as the Holy Spirit: Exodus separates pure beaten olive oil for the lamps (Ex 27:20) from compounded anointing oil (Ex 30:22–33); the virgins are told to buy oil that cannot be shared, while the Spirit is an unpurchasable gift (Acts 8:20); and the lamp–oil–light chain fits the commandment (Prov 6:23) becoming visible good works (Matt 5:16) via stored obedience. That much answers the dominant application of the common view to Matthew 25. However, the absolute claim that oil is ‘proven works 	o light; not the Spirit’ does not follow. The supplied texts never equate oil with works; the identification is an interpretive construction resting on the olive-tree = Israel link (Jer 11:16) plus the Gethsemane press image. More decisively, the argument never confronts the strongest counter-texts that do link oil (including lamp oil) to the Spirit—especially Zechariah 4:1–14, where olive oil continuously supplies the lampstand and is immediately explained as ‘not by might 	o but by my Spirit.’ The same omission applies to the anointing–Spirit cluster (1 Sam 16:13; Isa 61:1 / Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38). Distinguishing two recipes of oil does not erase those associations or make ‘oil’ generally mean proven works. Because a decisive counter-reading remains unanswered and the sources under-carry the universal redefinition, the book’s conclusion is not better supported than the common interpretation.
unresolved_objections: Zechariah 4 explicitly ties olive oil that feeds lamps to the Spirit, a parallel the chapter never addresses
Anointing oil (still olive-based) is repeatedly joined to the Spirit’s coming; the recipe distinction does not cancel the symbolic association
No text states ‘oil = proven works’; the equation is a multi-step symbolic chain that remains under-supported
Oil of gladness, medicinal oil, and agricultural blessing texts do not fit ‘proven works that make light’ yet are still ‘oil’
